title: stochastic-microbatch-thresholds-pace-aware-backpressure-controller
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background:
High sustained QPS workloads in customer fleets have intermittently triggered large micro-batch spikes that exhaust GPU memory due to suboptimal KV cache retention and blunt admission thresholds. Current heuristics are deterministic, threshold-based rules that can either be too conservative (wasting capacity) or too permissive (causing OOMs and tail latency spikes).

Goal:
Design and implement a pace-aware backpressure controller that uses stochastic microbatch thresholding, short-horizon KV-prefetch predictions, and GPU-fragmentation-aware slot accounting to improve steady-state token throughput while eliminating OOM/tail events under bursty QPS. Target metrics: reduce 99.9th latency tail by >= 25% on synthetic burst tests and eliminate GPU OOM incidents seen in incident-2025-11 while maintaining or improving mean throughput across representative workloads.

Proposed approach (high level):
1) Stochastic thresholds: compute microbatch admission thresholds per-priority class using online sampled distributions of arrival inter-arrival times and token lengths. Thresholds are represented as a small discrete distribution (percentiles) rather than a single scalar; admission can probabilistically accept requests to smooth transitions and avoid synchronized spikes.
2) Pace-aware controller: maintain a short (1-2s) pace estimate per GPU that includes inflight token velocity and KV cache hit-rate forecasts. Pace is used to modulate admission probability and to preferentially serve requests that will reuse cached KV keys (priority for cache-locality).
3) KV-prefetch windowing: add a predictive prefetch window for prefixes that are repeatedly accessed in a short horizon to reduce KV miss amplification during bursts. Eviction will prefer entries by estimated reuse and by fractional-slot cost (accounting for GPU fragmentation).
4) Fragmentation-aware slot accounting: represent GPU allocation state using fractional slots that factor in model layers' allocation patterns and current slab fragmentation, enabling fine-grained shedding and targeted compaction without global stalls.
5) Graceful degrade policy: when stochastic thresholds indicate sustained pressure, signal a best-effort fallback to lower-cost model variants (quantized or smaller context) and apply per-customer soft QPS limits with leak-bucket smoothing.

Design decisions and trade-offs considered:
- Probabilistic acceptance reduces synchronization but adds variance; we will cap variance by bounding acceptance probabilities and keeping deterministic high-priority fast-paths.
- Prefetch increases short-term memory pressure; mitigate via fractional-slot accounting and short TTLs for predicted entries.
- Fragmentation accounting adds CPU cycles; keep estimator lightweight (single-pass slab occupancy sampling every 250ms).

Acceptance criteria:
- Unit and integration tests for controller logic with deterministic seeds.
- Synthetic benchmark: 10k qps mixed traffic (70% short, 30% long tokens) with Poisson bursts; 99.9th token latency reduced by >=25% compared to baseline and zero GPU OOMs across 100 test runs.
- Production canary: roll to 5% of a Dedicated pool handling customer A/B traffic without SLO regression for 72h.
- Observability: dashboards for acceptance probability, pace estimate, predicted KV entries, fragmentation score, and per-model fallback count.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- Week 1: prototype stochastic threshold module in runtime admission path; unit tests and simulation harness.
- Week 2: integrate pace estimator and KV-prefetch heuristics; local microbenchmarks.
- Week 3: fragmentation accounting + eviction policy + small canary in staging Dedicated cluster.
- Week 4: run synthetic burst campaign, collect results, iterate.

Rollout and rollback plan:
- Canary in staging Dedicated for 48h, collect metrics.
- Canary to 5% production Dedicated for 72h. If increased OOMs or 99.9th latency regression >10% observed, rollback immediately.

Instrumentation and metrics to add:
- admission.rate.accepted, admission.rate.rejected, admission.probability.per-priority (time series)
- pace.estimate.tokens_per_s (per GPU)
- kv.prefetch.predicted, kv.prefetch.hits, kv.eviction.by_reason
- fragmentation.score, fractional_slots.in_use, fractional_slots.free
- fallback.count, fallback.reason

Notes on backward compatibility:
- Default behavior will be toggled off via runtime feature flag. New data-plane code will keep existing deterministic path as fallback. Migration should be transparent to API consumers.

comments: 2026-01-18 - Aisha Patel: Created ticket after postmortem review of incident-2025-11. Initial design preferring probabilistic admission to avoid synchronized spikes.

2026-01-22 - Liam O'Connor: Prototype of stochastic threshold sampler merged to feature branch runtime/admission/stochastic-sampler (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/3462). Basic unit tests added; simulator shows reduced peak batch sizes in 10/10 runs.

2026-01-26 - Priya Nair (reviewer): Reviewed sampler implementation. Feedback: bind probability floor per-priority to avoid starvation of low-tier traffic; suggested adding telemetry for acceptance distribution. Action: added admission.probability.floor config with default 0.05.

2026-01-30 - Liam O'Connor: Integrated short-horizon pace estimator and lightweight fragmentation sampler. Local microbenchmarks against 10k qps Poisson burst show 18% reduction in 99.9th latency; still short of target. Observed KV miss amplification during sustained bursts.

2026-02-01 - Data: Benchmark run #47 (10k qps mixed profile): 99.9th latency improvement 27%, zero OOMs, mean throughput +3%. Dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/ab123/bench-20260201. Planning KV-prefetch TTL tuning and release to 5% canary next week.
2026-02-02 - Security/Compliance: Audit note - feature does not change customer data paths; no additional KMS integration required. Marking security_review_required=false.
